passages.source_text: τινὶ γὰρ προφητείαν ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι θέλοντι ἐὰν συγχωρηθῇ πιστεύεσθαι ἐν οἷς ψεύστης φωρᾶται ὅτι τότε τὸ τῆς προγνώσεως ἅγιον οὐκ εἶχεν πνεῦμα, οὐκ εὐέλεγκτος ἔσται ψεύστης ὑπάρχων προφήτης· ἐν οἷς γὰρ ὡς πολλὰ λέγων ὀλίγα ἐπιτυγχάνει, τότε τὸ πνεῦμα ἔχειν πιστεύεται, ἔτι τε τὰ πρῶτα ἔσχατα λέγει, τὰ ἔσχατα πρῶτα, τὰ γενόμενα ὡς ἐσόμενα, τὰ ἐσόμενα ὡς ἤδη γεγονότα, ἄλλα καὶ ἀνακόλουθα καὶ ἐξ ἄλλων ὑφῃρημένα καὶ μεταμεμορφωμένα, ἃ δὲ μεμειωμένα, ἀνείδεα, ἀνόητα, ἀμφίβολα, λοξά, ἄδηλα, πάσης κεκραγότα δυσσυνειδησίας.

δεῖ δὲ καὶ ἐν ταῖς εὐχαῖς τὸ θεῷ προσπεφευγέναι ὁμολογεῖν, καὶ διαμαρτύρεσθαι τὴν τοῦ δαίμονος οὐκ ἀπείθειαν, ἀλλὰ βραδυτῆτα. πάντα γὰρ τῷ πιστεύοντι γίνεται, ἀπιστοῦντι δὲ οὐδέν. ὅθεν αὐτοὶ οἱ δαίμονες, εἰδότες ὧν ἐπικρατοῦσιν τῆς πίστεως τὴν ποσότητα, ἀναλογοῦσαν ἐπιμετροῦσιν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐπιμονήν. διὰ τοῦτο τοῖς ἀπιστοῦσιν ἐπιμένουσιν, τοῖς δὲ δυσπίστοις ἐνβραδύνουσιν, τοῖς δὲ παντάπασιν πιστεύσασι καὶ εὖ πράττουσιν οὐδὲ πρὸς ῥοπὴν ὥρας συνεῖναι δύνανται. ἡ γὰρ ψυχὴ τῇ πρὸς θεὸν πίστει ὡς εἰς ὕδατος φύσιν τραπεῖσα τὸν δαίμονα ὡς σπινθῆρα πυρὸς ἀποσβέννυσιν. κάματος οὖν ἐστὶν ἑκάστῳ ἐννοηθῆναι τὴν τοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ δαίμονος φυγήν. ἀνακιρνάμενοι γὰρ ταῖς ψυχαῖς, ὅπως τις τῆς αὐτοῦ σωτηρίας ἀμελήσῃ, ἐνθυμήσεις πρὸς ἃ βούλονται ὑποβάλλουσιν εἰς τὸν ἑκάστου νοῦν.

τινὲς δὲ τῶν κακούργων δαιμόνων ἄλλως ἐνεδρεύουσιν, τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ ὅτι εἰσὶν ἐνφαίνοντες, ὅπως ἡ κατ’ αὐτῶν σπουδὴ μὴ γένηται, εὐκαίρως δὲ ὀργῆς προφάσει, ἔρωτος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς ἤτοι ξίφει ἢ βρόχῳ ἢ κρημνῷ ἢ ἑτέρῳ τινὶ τὸ σῶμα αἰφνιδίως ἐνυβρίζουσιν, καὶ εἰς τέλος κολασθησομένας καθιστᾶσιν τῶν ἀνακεκραμένων τὰς ἠπατημένας αὐτοῖς ψυχάς, ὡς ἔφαμεν, εἰς τὸ καθάρσιον χωρήσαντες πῦρ. ἄλλοι δὲ ἄλλως ἐνεδρευόμενοι οὐ προσίασιν ἡμῖν, ταῖς τῶν κακούργων δαιμόνων ἐνθυμήσεσιν ἀπατώμενοι ὡς ὑπὸ μὲν τῶν θεῶν αὐτῶν ταῦτα πάσχοντες διὰ τὴν πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἀμέλειαν, θυσίαις δὲ αὐτοὺς διαλλάσσειν δυνάμενοι, καὶ ὅτι μὴ χρὴ αὐτοὺς ἡμῖν προσιέναι, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον φεύγειν καὶ μισεῖν. καὶ ὁμῶς μισοῦσιν καὶ φεύγουσιν τοὺς μᾶλλον ἐλεῶντας καὶ ἐπ’ εὐεργεσίᾳ αὐτοὺς διώκοντας.

ὁ γὰρ θεὸς πάντα δύναται. ἐκεῖνος γάρ ἐστιν ἀγαθὸς καὶ δίκαιος, νῦν πᾶσιν μακροθυμῶν, ἵνα οἱ βουλόμενοι ἐφ’ οἷς ἔπραξαν κακοῖς μεταμεληθέντες καὶ πολιτευσάμενοι, ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ᾗ τὰ πάντα κρίνεται, κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπολαύσωσιν. διὸ νῦν ἄρξασθε, ἀγαθῆς γνώσεως αἰτίᾳ θεῷ πειθόμενοι ἀντιλέγειν ὑμῶν ταῖς κακαῖς ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἐννοίαις, ἵνα δυνηθῆτε ἀνακαλέσασθαι τὴν πρώτην τῇ ἀνθρωπότητι παραδοθεῖσαν σωτήριον θρησκείαν. οὕτω γὰρ ὑμῖν ἐξαυτῆς ἀνατελεῖ τὰ ἀγαθά, ἅτινα λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν τοῦ λοιποῦ καταλείψετε. ἀλλὰ τῷ δεδωκότι εὐχαριστήσατε, μετὰ τοῦ τῆς εἰρήνης βασιλέως εἰσαεὶ τῶν ἀπορρήτων βασιλεύοντες ἀγαθῶν. ἐν δὲ τῷ παρόντι, ἀενάῳ ποταμῷ ἢ πηγῇ ἐπεί γε κἂν θαλάσσῃ ἀπολουσάμενοι ἐπὶ τῇ τρισμακαρίᾳ ἐπονομασίᾳ οὐ μόνον τὰ ἐνδομυχοῦντα ὑμῖν πνεύματα ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ θεῷ ἀνενδοιάστως πιστεύοντες τὰ ἄλλων κακὰ πνεύματα καὶ δαιμόνια χαλεπὰ σὺν τοῖς δεινοῖς πάθεσιν ἀπελάσετε. ἐνίοτε δὲ μόνον ἐνδόντων ὑμῶν φεύξονται· ἴσασιν γὰρ τοὺς ἀποδεδωκότας ἑαυτοὺς τῷ θεῷ, διὸ τιμῶντες αὐτοὺς πεφοβημένοι φεύγουσιν, ὥσπερ ἐχθὲς ἑωράκατε πῶς ἐμοῦ ἀναθεμένου μετὰ τὴν προσομιλίαν εὔξασθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν πασχόντων αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν, βραχεῖαν ὥραν στέξαι μὴ δυνηθέντα.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Πολὺ συμβάλλεται πρὸς νίκην τῷ πολεμοῦντι τὸ ἰδίοις χρήσασθαι ὅπλοις. ὃ γὰρ φιλεῖ τις: καὶ γνησίως ἐκδικεῖν δύναται, γνησίως δὲ ἐκδικούμενον οὐ τὴν τυχοῦσαν ἰσχὺν ἔχει. διὸ τοῦ λοιποῦ ὅπερ ὄντως φρονῶ ἐκθήσομαι. φημί τινα δύναμιν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις εἶναι ἄγνωστον πᾶσι, καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ δημιουργῷ (ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἴρηκεν, οὐκ ἐπιστάμενος ὃ ἐφθέγξατο· ἐκ πολυλαλίας γὰρ ἐνίοτε εὐστοχεῖ τις πρὸς τὸ ἀληθές, οὐκ εἰδὼς ὃ λέγει). λέγω δὲ καὶ περὶ τούτου οὗ εἴρηκεν „οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα“. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σὺ τὰ ἐκείνου εἰδέναι μηκέτι ἐπαγγέλλου. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Τὰ ἐκείνου οὐκ ἐπαγγέλλομαι πιστεύειν, εἰς δὲ τὰ ἐπιτευχθέντα αὐτῷ διαλέγομαί σοι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἵνα μή σοι δῶ πρόφασιν εἰς φυγήν, ζητήσω σοι ὡς θέλεις· πλὴν μαρτύρομαι πάντας ὅτι οὐδὲ ὃν νῦν ἔφης λόγον, οὐ πιστεύεις. οἶδα γὰρ ἃ φρονεῖς. καὶ ἵνα μή με δόξῃς ψεύδεσθαι, αἰνίξομαί σοι τὰ σά, ἵνα ἴδῃς ὅτι πρὸς εἰδότα διαλέγῃ.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: For if someone wishing to profess prophecy is allowed to have it believed, in the matters in which he is caught as a liar, that at that time he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge, he will not be easy to expose, though he is a prophet who is a liar. For in the cases where, while saying many things, he hits upon a few, he is then believed to have the spirit. Moreover, he speaks of first things as last and last things as first, things that have happened as things that will happen, and things that will happen as though they had already happened. He also says other, incoherent things, things stolen from others and transformed, and some things curtailed, shapeless, senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear, all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τῆς προγνώσεως ἅγιον οὐκ εἶχεν πνεῦμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s attributive relation between the holy spirit and foreknowledge without imposing a later doctrinal identification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while saying many things, he hits upon a few
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτυγχάνει describes occasionally hitting the mark or obtaining a correct result among numerous claims.

lexical_decisions.chosen: things stolen from others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφαιρέω can mean taking something away secretly; “appropriated from others” is a less pointed alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: curtailed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive describes things reduced, diminished, or mutilated; “curtailed” fits the treatment of allegedly defective predictions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shapeless
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed spelling supports ἀνειδής, “without form, shapeless, unsightly,” rather than ἀναιδής, “shameless.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεκραγότα vividly portrays the statements as openly betraying or proclaiming something; δυσσυνειδησία can denote a bad or guilty conscience and, by extension, unscrupulousness.

passages.text: And in prayers one must also confess that one has taken refuge in God and solemnly affirm that, on the demon’s part, it is not disobedience but delay. For everything comes to pass for the one who believes, but nothing for the one who does not believe. Hence the demons themselves, knowing the quantity of faith possessed by those whom they overpower, allot a proportionate measure of their own persistence. For this reason they persist with those who do not believe, linger with those who have difficulty believing, but cannot remain even for an instant with those who have believed completely and act well. For the soul, having been turned by faith toward God as though into the nature of water, extinguishes the demon like a spark of fire. It is therefore difficult for each person to recognize the flight of the demon within them. For the demons, blending themselves with souls so that a person may neglect their own salvation, suggest to each person’s mind thoughts directed toward whatever they wish.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that one has taken refuge in God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect infinitive presents recourse to God as an accomplished act with a continuing state.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not disobedience but delay
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast concerns the demon’s delayed departure rather than outright refusal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the quantity of faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording explicitly presents faith as possessing a measurable degree or amount.

lexical_decisions.chosen: linger with those who have difficulty believing
lexical_decisions.rationale: δύσπιστος denotes difficulty or reluctance in believing, distinguished here from outright unbelief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: It is therefore difficult
lexical_decisions.rationale: κάματος literally denotes labor or weariness and here characterizes recognition as laborious or difficult.

passages.text: Some of the wicked demons lie in wait in another way. At first they do not even reveal that they exist, so that no effort against them may arise; but at an opportune moment, under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else, they suddenly assault the body by a sword, a noose, a precipice, or some other means. And they bring it about that the deceived souls of those who have been mingled with them will be punished to the end, as we said, after they—the demons—have entered the purifying fire. Others, being ambushed in another way, do not approach us, because they are deceived by the thoughts of the wicked demons into supposing that they suffer these things from their own gods because of their neglect toward them, that they can reconcile those gods through sacrifices, and that they must not approach us but, on the contrary, must flee and hate us. And all the same, they hate and flee those who have greater compassion for them and pursue them in order to benefit them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ ὅτι εἰσὶν ἐνφαίνοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: At first they do not even reveal that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὴν ἀρχήν can mean “at the beginning” or idiomatically “at all”; the subsequent reference to an opportune occasion favors a temporal contrast.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀργῆς προφάσει, ἔρωτος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως here denotes passionate or erotic desire, while πρόφασις presents these emotions as pretexts or occasions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they suddenly assault the body
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνυβρίζω conveys violent mistreatment or outrage against the body.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they bring it about that ... will be punished to the end
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future passive participle κολασθησομένας gives the punishment prospective force. εἰς τέλος may mean “to the end,” “completely,” or, in some contexts, “forever”; the source-transparent wording leaves its extent unresolved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after they—the demons—have entered the purifying fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: χωρήσαντες is nominative masculine plural and most directly resumes the demons as grammatical subject. A contextual association with the people mingled with them is possible despite the case difference.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And all the same
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμῶς can mean “alike” or “all the same”; the latter preserves the ironic contrast with the compassion shown to them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἀνακεκραμένων τὰς ἠπατημένας αὐτοῖς ψυχάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the deceived souls of those who have been mingled with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main wording attaches αὐτοῖς to the more distant mingling participle, supported by the blending of demons with souls described immediately before in9.11. A material alternative attaches it to the nearer deceived participle: the souls deceived by them, belonging to those who have been mingled. The main text does not claim its longer-distance attachment is uniquely established, and no correction to the supplied Greek is proposed.

passages.text: For God can do everything. He is good and just, showing patience toward everyone now, so that those who are willing, after regretting the evil deeds they committed and living accordingly, may, on the day when everything is judged, receive what they deserve. Therefore begin now, obeying God, the cause of good knowledge, to oppose your evil desires and thoughts, so that you may recover for yourselves the original saving religion handed down to humanity. In this way good things will immediately spring up for you; once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils. But give thanks to the one who gave them, reigning forever with the King of Peace over the inexpressible good things. At present, after washing yourselves in an ever-flowing river or spring, or indeed even in the sea, with the thrice-blessed invocation, you will not only be able to drive away the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses, but—if you yourselves no longer sin and believe God without wavering—you will drive out other people’s evil spirits and fierce demons, together with their dreadful afflictions. Sometimes, however, they will flee when you merely yield. For they recognize those who have given themselves to God, and therefore, showing them honor, they flee in fear. Just as yesterday you saw how, when I had put off praying for those who were suffering until after the discourse, the afflictions themselves cried aloud because of the honor paid to the religion, unable to endure for even a short time.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after regretting
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes regret or a changed concern regarding the evils committed. It is kept distinct from the μετανοέω terminology governed by the reorientation policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and living accordingly
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεύομαι concerns conducting one’s life. “Accordingly” expresses the contextual connection with regret; the more formally literal alternative is “and having conducted their lives.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: obeying God, the cause of good knowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative αἰτίᾳ is taken in apposition to θεῷ, identifying God as the cause of good knowledge. Other possible attachments are “because of good knowledge, obeying God” and “for the sake of good knowledge, obeying God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πρώτην τῇ ἀνθρωπότητι παραδοθεῖσαν σωτήριον θρησκείαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the original saving religion handed down to humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρώτην characterizes the religion as first or original, while σωτήριον describes it as saving. The wording preserves the author’s historical claim without harmonization.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν τοῦ λοιποῦ καταλείψετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: The chosen attachment takes ἅτινα, referring to the good things, as the object of λαβόντες and πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν as the object of καταλείψετε. A grammatically possible alternative joins λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν, “having experienced evils,” and takes ἅτινα as the object of καταλείψετε: “which, after experiencing evils, you will thereafter leave behind.” That alternative would make the promised good things what is abandoned and is therefore contextually difficult.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the thrice-blessed invocation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπονομασία can mean naming, designation, or invocation. In the washing context, “invocation” conveys an enacted naming formula without supplying words not quoted in the source.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ μόνον τὰ ἐνδομυχοῦντα ὑμῖν πνεύματα ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ θεῷ ἀνενδοιάστως πιστεύοντες τὰ ἄλλων κακὰ πνεύματα καὶ δαιμόνια χαλεπὰ σὺν τοῖς δεινοῖς πάθεσιν ἀπελάσετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you will not only be able to drive away the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses, but—if you yourselves no longer sin and believe God without wavering—you will drive out other people’s evil spirits and fierce demons, together with their dreadful afflictions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first member explicitly expresses ability with ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, whereas the second uses the direct future ἀπελάσετε. The English therefore does not extend “be able” over the second expulsion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or hiding deep within and preserves the source’s spatial image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when you merely yield
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute uses ἐνδίδωμι in the intransitive sense “yield” or “give way.” In context it may mean yielding oneself to God, as the following clause about self-dedication suggests; “when you merely consent” or “when you merely permit it” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the afflictions themselves cried aloud
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, a regular Greek construction. The personification, or identification of the afflictions with their spiritual agents, is preserved rather than explained away.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐμοῦ ἀναθεμένου μετὰ τὴν προσομιλίαν εὔξασθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν πασχόντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: when I had put off praying for those who were suffering until after the discourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ἀναθεμένου as postponing or reserving the prayer and attaches after the discourse to its intended time. This fits the following inability of the afflictions to endure even the brief delay. A material alternative takes the verb as undertaking: when after the discourse I undertook to pray for those who were suffering. That places the undertaking after the discourse rather than depicting the prayer as deferred. Both lexical and temporal choices are disclosed; the verified Greek has not been corrected.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the afflictions themselves cried aloud because of the honor paid to the religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main causal dative leaves the source of the honor unexpressed. A material alternative is cried aloud out of respect for the religion, taking the afflictions or their spiritual agents themselves as showing reverence, supported by the immediately preceding demons showing honor. Neither identifies a new explicit honor-giver, and the personification of the afflictions remains intact.

passages.text: Simon said, “For a combatant, using his own weapons contributes greatly to victory. For what someone loves he can also genuinely defend, and what is genuinely defended possesses no ordinary strength. Therefore from now on I will set out what I really think. I say that there is a certain power in secrecy, unknown to everyone, even to the maker himself—as Jesus himself also said, without knowing what he uttered; for sometimes, through much talking, someone hits upon the truth without knowing what he says. I am also speaking about this statement he made: ‘No one knew the Father.’” Peter said, “No longer claim to know his teachings.” Simon said, “I do not claim to believe his teachings; I am debating with you about the things he happened to get right.” Peter said, “So as not to give you an excuse to flee, I will discuss with you as you wish. Nevertheless I call everyone to witness that you do not believe even the argument you have now stated. For I know what you think. And so that you do not think I am lying, I will hint at your own views, so that you may see you are conversing with someone who knows.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: what someone loves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object can be a position or cause, not necessarily a person; this introduces the own-weapons metaphor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things he happened to get right
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves Simon’s disparaging account of accidental truth rather than endorsing his claim as a narrator’s assessment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λέγω δὲ καὶ περὶ τούτου οὗ εἴρηκεν „οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα“.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am also speaking about this statement he made: No one knew the Father
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes τούτου as this statement and οὗ as a relative attracted into the antecedent's genitive case, referring to what he uttered. The surrounding discussion of Jesus' words and the quotation supplying their content favor that reading. A material personal alternative is I am also speaking about this one of whom he said, No one knew the Father, potentially linking the Father to the previously mentioned unknown power. The main text does not claim that this statement rather than a personal referent is uniquely established.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
